questions.q: What problem does cluster DNS solve that a Service's stable virtual IP alone does not?
options: A stable IP alone doesn't tell every other Pod what that IP actually is — DNS gives the Service a predictable name any Pod can resolve
Services don't actually have a ClusterIP without DNS enabled
DNS replaces the need for kube-proxy entirely
DNS is only needed for Services with type LoadBalancer
questions.explain: A Service's virtual IP is stable, but something still has to communicate that IP to every Pod that needs it. CoreDNS gives each Service a predictable name, so Pods resolve a name to an IP instead of hard-coding it.

questions.q: What is CoreDNS, as described in this lesson?
options: A command-line tool for writing YAML Ingress rules
The in-cluster DNS server, typically run as a Deployment in kube-system, that answers name lookups for Services
A replacement for the Kubernetes API server
A field inside every Pod spec that disables networking
questions.explain: CoreDNS runs in-cluster, usually in kube-system, fronted by its own Service (conventionally named kube-dns), and watches the API for Services and Endpoints to keep its DNS records current automatically.

questions.q: In the fully qualified name payments-api.billing.svc.cluster.local, what does the "svc" segment indicate?
options: The name of the container image being used
The version of the Kubernetes API in use
A fixed segment meaning this record refers to a Service
The name of the Ingress controller handling the request
questions.explain: The FQDN is built as service.namespace.svc.cluster.local — "svc" is a fixed, literal segment marking the record as a Service, distinct from, say, a Pod record.

questions.q: Why can a Pod in the billing namespace reach payments-api with no suffix, while a Pod in the checkout namespace cannot?
options: Because checkout Pods have DNS disabled by default
Because payments-api only exists as a NodePort, not a ClusterIP
Because cross-namespace traffic is always blocked by a default NetworkPolicy
Because Kubernetes configures each Pod's DNS search path to include its own namespace first, so short names only resolve correctly from the same namespace
questions.explain: Each Pod's resolv.conf search path starts with its own namespace, which is why a bare Service name resolves correctly only when the caller is in that same namespace — a cross-namespace caller needs at least service.namespace.

questions.q: What does running kubectl exec -it dnsutils -- nslookup payments-api.billing.svc.cluster.local help you verify?
options: Whether the Ingress controller is correctly installed
Whether CoreDNS can resolve that name and what IP it returns, which you can compare against the Service's real ClusterIP
Whether the node has enough CPU to schedule new Pods
Whether the Deployment's rolling update strategy is configured correctly
questions.explain: nslookup from inside a debug Pod confirms whether CoreDNS answers for that name at all, and what IP comes back — checked against kubectl get svc to confirm it matches the real ClusterIP.
